claims.text: The initial Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are solid, chemically homogeneous, single-phase solid solutions.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles increases local configurational entropy.
The proposed configurational-entropy enhancement is especially pronounced at the nanoparticle surface.
Increased local configurational entropy reduces local cohesive energies.
The mixture of atomic species produces spatial variation in surface bonding and regions of lower cohesive energy.
Reduced-cohesion surface regions undergo localized atomic disorder before the whole particle melts.
Localized surface disorder progressively permeates the nanoparticle during heating.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles consequently have a spatially heterogeneous melting transition.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles have a broader temperature interval between initial surface disordering and complete melting than simpler nanoparticles.
A chemically homogeneous Fe–Ni binary nanoparticle is expected to exhibit a sharper and more uniform melting transition than the HEA nanoparticle.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to random-solid-solution nanoparticles in the tens-of-nanometers size range.
Strong size effects can confound the predicted broadening of melting.
Phase separation can confound the predicted broadening of melting.
The predicted temperature span and magnitude of surface disorder depend on nanoparticle size, simulation parameters, and the chosen interatomic potential.
Direct extrapolation from the proposed simulations to experimental conditions may be unreliable.
